# MEMORANDUM

**To:** Supervising Partner
**From:** [Associate]
**Date:** November 5, 2026
**Re:** Stipuv Vertical Holdings, LLC – Post-Closing Review of Lockwen Lift Services Acquisition Documents (Matter s14-m0003)
**Privileged & Confidential – Attorney Work Product**

---

## I. Summary and Items Requiring Immediate Client Attention

We act for Stipuv Vertical Holdings, LLC (**Stipuv** or **Buyer**), the buyer under the Stock Purchase Agreement dated June 30, 2026 (the **SPA**) and the maker of the Subordinated Promissory Note (the **Seller Note** or **Note**). The deal is already closed. Stipuv acquired all of the stock of Lockwen Lift Services, Inc. (**Lockwen** or the **Company**) from Braveirt Elevator Group, Inc. (**Braveirt** or **Seller**) on June 30, 2026. The Purchase Price was $48,500,000, paid as $41,000,000 in cash (before deductions) and a **$7,500,000** Seller Note.

Because the deal has closed, our "fixes" are mostly:
- amendments that must be negotiated with Braveirt;
- waivers or extensions; and
- protective steps Stipuv can take on its own.

I found four significant issues, plus several lesser points. **Three matters are time-critical and should go to the client this week:**

1. **The Notice of Disagreement deadline has already passed (Issue 2).** Stipuv received the Closing Statement on August 4, 2026. The 30-day window under SPA §2.4(b) therefore closed on **September 3, 2026**. The managers did not authorize the objection until September 14, 2026. Braveirt can treat the **$1,240,000** working capital surplus as final and binding. We need to confirm today whether a notice has gone out, and pursue a written extension or waiver.

2. **General representation claims expire December 30, 2026 (Issue 3).** That is about eight weeks away. Every known or suspected claim must be noticed before then. This includes the elevator code compliance (§4.12), customer contract (§4.9) and undisclosed liability / deferred revenue matters. Claims not noticed by that date are lost, and so is the ability to set them off against the Note.

3. **The Seller Guarantee indemnity is uncapped (Issue 1).** Stipuv's indemnity of Braveirt's parent guarantees and bonds has no cap and reaches pre-closing defaults. Stipuv should immediately:
   - inventory the Seller Guarantees and any known pre-closing performance problems; and
   - start the replacement and release process.

## II. Ranked Issues

### Issue 1 (Most Significant): Uncapped Buyer Indemnity for Seller Guarantees, Including Pre-Closing Defaults

**Where:** SPA §9.3(b), read with §9.5(a), §9.5(c), §6.8 and the definition of "Seller Guarantees" in §1.1.

**What the documents say:**
- **§9.3(b).** Buyer indemnifies the Seller Indemnitees for all Losses arising from "any Seller Guarantee, including any demand, draw or claim made by any beneficiary... *whether arising before, on or after the Closing Date*."
- **"Seller Guarantees."** These are Braveirt's parent performance and payment guarantees, surety and performance bonds and other credit support that back Lockwen's maintenance, repair and modernization contracts (Schedule 6.8).
- **§9.5(a).** This caps each party's aggregate liability at **10% of the Purchase Price ($4,850,000)**. On its face the cap applies to Buyer's liability "under Section 9.3."
- **§9.5(c).** This then provides that "the limitations in this Section 9.5 *shall not apply to Losses under Section 9.3(b)*." That removes the cap entirely for Seller Guarantee Losses.
- **§6.8.** Buyer need only use "reasonable efforts" to obtain releases. There is no outside date, so Braveirt keeps the guarantees in place and Stipuv's exposure runs as long as the underlying contracts run.

**Why it matters to Stipuv:**
- **The risk allocation is inverted.** Suppose a building owner calls a Seller Guarantee or bond because of a performance failure that happened before Closing (for example, missed Category 1 or Category 5 tests, or a defective modernization job). Braveirt pays, then passes the full amount to Stipuv under §9.3(b) with no ceiling.
- **Stipuv's claim back against Braveirt for the same default is weak.** That claim would be a breach of §4.9 or §4.12 under §9.2(a). It is:
  - capped at $4,850,000;
  - subject to the $485,000 basket in §9.5(b); and
  - extinguished if not noticed by December 30, 2026 (see Issue 3).
- **The result is that Stipuv is the uncapped, indefinite insurer of Lockwen's pre-closing performance.** That risk was priced into the deal as Seller's.
- **The exposure may be large.** Modernization performance bonds commonly run to the full contract value.
- **There is a timing mismatch with the Note.** Set-off under §9.7 runs only for Buyer Indemnitee claims. A Seller claim under §9.3(b) is payable in cash on demand.

**Recommended fixes:**

1. **Negotiate an amendment to §9.3(b) and §9.5(c)** (a §11.5 written amendment signed by both parties). Proposed language:
   > "(b) any Seller Guarantee, solely to the extent the Losses arise out of any act, omission, event or circumstance first occurring after the Closing Date and not resulting from any inaccuracy in or breach of any representation or warranty of Seller or any act or omission of the Company prior to the Closing; *provided* that Seller shall indemnify the Buyer Indemnitees for all Losses under any Seller Guarantee to the extent arising out of any act, omission, event or circumstance occurring on or prior to the Closing Date."

   Also amend §9.5(c) either to delete the 9.3(b) carve-out or to substitute a specific cap. Add an outside date, for example: "Buyer's obligations under Section 9.3(b) shall terminate as to any Seller Guarantee on the earlier of its release and [24] months after the Closing Date."

2. **Strengthen §6.8 so the release obligation is reciprocal and Seller cooperates.** Braveirt should be required to cooperate in substituting the guarantees. Any guarantee not released by an outside date should be handled through a defined process, not left as indefinite exposure.

3. **Practical steps now:**
   - Have Lockwen begin offering replacement Stipuv or Company guarantees and bonds to the beneficiaries (this also performs Stipuv's §6.8 covenant).
   - Respect the §6.8 restriction on extending, renewing or amending guaranteed contracts.

4. **Defensive step before December 30, 2026.** Deliver a protective Claim Notice under §9.4 for any known or suspected pre-closing performance defaults under guaranteed contracts. This preserves the §9.2(a) cross-claim and the set-off.

**Leverage:** Braveirt wants to be released from the guarantees. Stipuv can offer an accelerated replacement program in exchange for limiting §9.3(b) to post-closing events.

---

### Issue 2: The Notice of Disagreement Window Expired Before the Managers Acted

**Where:** Buyer Managers' Written Consent dated September 14, 2026, Recital B (receipt on August 4, 2026), Recital C ("has not yet delivered" a Notice of Disagreement) and Resolution 2. Read with SPA §2.4(b), (c) and (d).

**What the documents say:**
- **SPA §2.4(b).** Buyer must deliver a Notice of Disagreement "within 30 days after Buyer's receipt of the Closing Statement." Otherwise "the Closing Statement shall be final and binding on the parties." Any item not specifically disputed in a timely notice is also final.
- **Recital B.** Stipuv received the Closing Statement on **August 4, 2026**. The 30-day period therefore expired on **September 3, 2026**. That date was a Thursday and not a holiday, so no extension applies.
- **Recital C.** Stipuv "has not yet delivered" a Notice of Disagreement. Resolution 2 authorizes one 11 days after the deadline. The proposed objection is that unearned deferred revenue on prepaid maintenance contracts was wrongly excluded from current liabilities.
- **The resulting surplus payable to Braveirt is $1,240,000.**
- **SPA §2.4(d).** The adjustment is payable within five Business Days after final determination.

**Why it matters to Stipuv:**
- Braveirt can argue that the Closing Statement became final and binding on September 3, 2026, and that the $1,240,000 became payable around September 10, 2026.
- On management's analysis, the surplus may be largely or entirely overstated.
- **Resolution 5 creates a conflict.** It forbids payment until "final determination." If Braveirt is right that determination has already occurred, withholding payment exposes Stipuv to a breach claim.
- The consent shows that Stipuv disputes the figure and has not accepted it. However, the SPA does not make that a ground for extension.
- I would not advise the client that the notice can still be delivered in time. It cannot.

**Recommended actions:**

1. **Confirm the facts immediately:**
   - whether and when the Notice of Disagreement authorized by Resolution 2 was actually delivered, and by what §11.2 method;
   - whether any written communication sent to Braveirt on or before September 3 disputed the deferred revenue item "in reasonable detail" (for example, finance team emails or advisor correspondence). If so, that communication may itself qualify as a timely notice; and
   - whether "receipt" on August 4 was of a complete Closing Statement with the "reasonable supporting documentation" §2.4(a) requires. If not, the 30-day clock arguably started later.

2. **If no notice has gone out, deliver it now.** It should comply with Resolution 2 and §2.4(b) and expressly reserve all rights. At the same time, ask Braveirt for a **written extension or waiver** under §11.5, deeming the notice timely. Braveirt may agree in exchange for faster resolution or other concessions.

3. **Develop fallback arguments.** None of these is certain, and each needs further work:
   - **Non-conforming statement.** §2.4(a) requires a "good-faith" statement "prepared in accordance with the Accounting Principles." A statement that departs from those principles may not have triggered the clock at all, or may support a bad-faith or manifest-error argument.
   - **Indemnity claim.** A §9.2(a) claim could be framed around §4.5, §4.6 and §4.9 (prepaid maintenance fees must be listed in Disclosure Schedule §4.9). It must be noticed before December 30, 2026. The §9.5(e) "no double recovery" rule and the §9.6 carve-out for §2.4 disputes will be raised against it.
   - **Fraud.** Fraud is defined narrowly in §1.1 and is limited to the making of representations.

4. **Board process going forward.** Calendar contractual deadlines on receipt of any deal notice, so that board action does not lag behind contractual windows.

---

### Issue 3: The Six-Month Survival Period Ends Long Before Any Set-Off Is Available

**Where:** SPA §9.1, read with §9.4(a), §9.7, the definition of "Fundamental Representations" in §1.1, and Seller Note §2(a) and §5(a).

**What the documents say:**
- **SPA §9.1.** Non-fundamental representations survive only until "*six (6) months after the Closing Date*," which is **December 30, 2026**.
- **Fundamental Representations.** These are limited to §4.1, §4.2, §4.3 and §4.20. The operationally critical representations survive only six months. These include:
  - §4.12 (Elevator Code Compliance and Permits);
  - §4.9 (Material Customer Contracts);
  - §4.5 and §4.6 (financial statements and undisclosed liabilities); and
  - §4.11, §4.15 and §4.18.
- **SPA §9.4(a).** A Claim Notice must be delivered before the survival date.
- **No escrow.** Set-off against the Note under SPA §9.7 is Stipuv's practical recovery source.
- **Note timing.** The first Note installment ($2,500,000 plus accrued interest at 6%) is not due until **December 31, 2027**. Note §5(a) limits set-off to claims "timely asserted by a Claim Notice... before the expiration of the applicable survival period."

**Why it matters to Stipuv:**
- Code compliance and permit defects typically surface through the annual periodic inspection and testing cycle and NYC DOB and NYS DOL filings. That cycle largely falls after December 30, 2026.
- The representations will therefore expire about a year before Stipuv can withhold any payment.
- For practical purposes, Stipuv has paid $7,500,000 of deferred consideration with no meaningful protection for the risks most specific to an elevator contractor.
- This also feeds Issue 1: once the representations lapse, Stipuv has no cross-claim against Braveirt for pre-closing defaults that Braveirt can pass back to Stipuv uncapped.

**Recommended fixes:**

1. **Before December 30, 2026 (protective):**
   - Commission an expedited compliance sweep of Lockwen's inspection and test records, DOB and DOL filings, open violations and customer complaints. Mr. Okafor-Wyse's role under Key Employee Agreement §3(b) makes him the natural point person.
   - Deliver Claim Notices under §9.4(a) describing in reasonable detail every known or suspected breach, with estimated Losses where possible. At a minimum, cover §4.12, §4.9 (including the deferred revenue and prepaid fee disclosure point) and §4.6.
   - A noticed claim survives until resolved and can then be set off against the Note.

2. **Negotiate an amendment to §9.1.** Extend survival for §4.5, §4.6, §4.9, §4.11 and §4.12 to the later of 18 months after Closing and 30 days after the first Note installment. Proposed language:
   > "The representations and warranties in Sections 4.5, 4.6, 4.9, 4.11 and 4.12 shall survive the Closing until the later of (i) eighteen (18) months after the Closing Date and (ii) January 31, 2028."

   Conform Note §5(a) to match. In the alternative, seek an escrow or holdback.

3. **Leverage.** Pair this request with Stipuv's concessions on the Seller Guarantee replacement (Issue 1) and the Closing Statement extension (Issue 2).

---

### Issue 4: The Seller Note Is Freely Assignable and Negotiable, and Set-Off Runs Only Against "Seller"

**Where:** Seller Note §8(a), read with Note §1 ("to the order of Holder"), the definition of "Holder," §5 and §7, and SPA §9.7, §11.6 and §11.9.

**What the documents say:**
- **Note §8(a).** Holder may "sell, assign, transfer, pledge or negotiate this Note... to any Person *without the consent of Maker*." The only requirement is notice to Stipuv within 10 Business Days afterward. Competitors are not excluded.
- **Set-off scope.** Note §5 permits set-off only against amounts "payable to Seller," and SPA §9.7 against amounts payable "by Buyer to Seller." Neither provision states that set-off binds any assignee or Holder.
- **Negotiability.** Note §1 is drafted as an order instrument ("pay to the order of Holder"), and §11 waives presentment and notice of dishonor.
- **SPA §11.6** restricts assignment of "this Agreement" only. It does not reach the Note.
- **SPA §11.9** (order of precedence) resolves only conflicts, and there is no conflicting SPA provision on Note transfers.
- **Note §7** gives "Holder" monthly financial statements and monthly schedules of every Lockwen contract, showing:
  - counterparty and building location;
  - annual value; and
  - expiration and renewal notice dates.

**Why it matters to Stipuv:**
- **Loss of set-off.** A transferee, especially one claiming holder-in-due-course status under NY UCC Article 3, may take free of Stipuv's set-off and recoupment defenses. That would remove Stipuv's principal indemnity recovery source (see Issue 3).
- **The negotiability analysis is uncertain.** The Note's references to the Purchase Agreement and its conditional set-off provisions may defeat negotiability. However, Stipuv should not have to litigate the point.
- **Competitive harm.** A competing elevator maintenance contractor could buy the Note. It would then receive Lockwen's customer, pricing and renewal data monthly, which is precisely what it needs to poach accounts at renewal.
- **Gaps in Seller's covenants.** The SPA §6.2 confidentiality and §6.3 and §6.4 non-compete and non-solicit covenants bind only Braveirt and its Affiliates, not an unaffiliated transferee.

**Recommended fixes (amend and restate the Note, signed by Maker and Holder under Note §11):**

1. **Revise §8(a) as follows:**
   > "Holder may not sell, assign, transfer, pledge or negotiate this Note, in whole or in part, without the prior written consent of Maker, which shall not be unreasonably withheld, except that no consent may be given to, and no transfer shall be made to, any Person (or Affiliate of any Person) engaged in the Business. Any purported transfer in violation of this Section 8(a) shall be void."

   A narrow exception for a collateral pledge to Braveirt's bank lender may be acceptable, provided the bank takes subject to these terms.

2. **Make the Note non-negotiable.** Add a legend: "THIS NOTE IS NOT A NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENT." Replace "to the order of Holder" with "to Seller or its permitted assigns."

3. **Make set-off binding on all holders.** Amend Note §5 and SPA §9.7:
   > "The rights of Maker under this Section 5 shall be binding upon, and enforceable against, Seller and every subsequent Holder, each of which takes this Note subject to all rights of set-off, recoupment and defense of Maker under this Note and the Purchase Agreement, whether arising before or after any transfer."

   Replace references to "Seller" with "Holder" where payments are concerned.

4. **Limit §7 information rights.** Give transferees only summary financials, not contract schedules. Condition delivery on a confidentiality undertaking.

5. **Ask Braveirt now** whether it has transferred or pledged the Note. Confirm that no §8(a) transfer notice has been received.

6. **Use the senior lender.** Any subordination agreement under Note §6(c) with Stipuv's senior lender is an opportunity to impose transfer restrictions, since lenders often require them.

## III. Other Observations (Lower Priority)

**Key Employee Agreement (Darnell Okafor-Wyse)**
- **Incentive equity covenant.** Under §5(d) and §13, Stipuv (as Parent) must recommend a profits interest grant to its Board, to be considered within 90 days after the Effective Date, i.e., by **September 28, 2026**.
  - Confirm that this happened. The September 14 consent does not address it.
  - If it did not happen, Stipuv is in breach of a covenant it signed. Mr. Okafor-Wyse is central to Lockwen's code compliance, so the relationship matters.
- **Term and retention.** The Initial Term runs two years from Closing, to June 30, 2028, with automatic one-year renewals unless notice is given 90 days before expiry. The $150,000 retention bonus is payable in two installments after the first and second anniversaries.
  - Calendar the non-renewal notice date (around April 1, 2028).
  - Severance is 12 months' base salary ($245,000) plus COBRA, triggered by termination without Cause or resignation for Good Reason.
- **Restrictive covenants.** The 12-month non-compete extends to counties in NJ and CT. Enforceability depends on the governing law and reasonableness. Monitor developments in New York non-compete legislation. The §9(d) reformation clause helps.
- **Insider compliance risk.** Mr. Okafor-Wyse oversaw pre-closing compliance. His knowledge is relevant to the §4.12 claim sweep in Issue 3. Handle any interviews with care.

**Broker cover letter (Pellucid Risk Partners)**
- This letter is largely administrative. It confirms that Lockwen's policies were in force on June 30, 2026, that Stipuv has been added as an additional insured on the GL, umbrella and auto policies, and that premiums are paid.
- The certificates are "information only" (§5.1–5.2). Request copies of the policies and endorsements to verify the additional insured wording.
- Confirm which pre-closing occurrences fall under Braveirt's own policies, given Seller's cooperation covenant in SPA §6.9. That may help offset Seller Guarantee losses.
- Under SPA §9.5(d), any insurance proceeds reduce indemnifiable Losses.

**Seller Note: other points**
- Note §9(d) makes a sale of the Company or its assets an Event of Default unless the Note is repaid. This is relevant to exit planning.
- §5(b) withheld amounts are repayable "to Seller." Conform this when amending.

## IV. Further Information and Documents Needed

1. Schedule 6.8 (Seller Guarantees): each guarantee and bond, its beneficiary, amount, expiry, and any pending or threatened demands.
2. The Closing Statement as delivered, with its cover communication and supporting documents, and evidence of the August 4 receipt and delivery method.
3. All communications with Braveirt about the Closing Statement, and whether and when the Resolution 2 Notice of Disagreement was delivered.
4. Schedules 1.1(a) and 1.1(b) (Accounting Principles and illustrative working capital calculation) and the Estimated Closing Statement, to evaluate the deferred revenue position.
5. The Disclosure Schedule, especially §4.9 (prepaid maintenance fees), §4.12 (Permits) and §4.13.
6. Lockwen's DOB and DOL inspection, test and violation records since January 1, 2023, and any customer complaints or default notices.
7. Any §8(a) transfer notice for the Note, and Stipuv's senior credit documents (for Senior Indebtedness and subordination terms).
8. Stipuv's LLC Agreement and board minutes on the §5(d) profits interest recommendation.
9. Lockwen's insurance policies and endorsements, and Braveirt's occurrence-based policies covering Lockwen before Closing.

## V. Proposed Next Steps

| Priority | Action | Deadline |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Confirm whether the Notice of Disagreement was delivered. If not, deliver it and request a written extension or waiver from Braveirt. | Immediately |
| 2 | Run the compliance sweep and deliver protective Claim Notices (§4.5, §4.6, §4.9, §4.11, §4.12), including for Seller Guarantee-related pre-closing defaults. | Well before December 30, 2026 |
| 3 | Inventory the Seller Guarantees and launch the replacement program. | Within 30 days |
| 4 | Open a negotiation package with Braveirt: limit §9.3(b) and remove the §9.5(c) carve-out; extend survival; amend Note §5 and §8; resolve the working capital timing point. | Following client sign-off |
| 5 | Confirm compliance with KEA §5(d). | Within 2 weeks |

Please let me know if you would like draft language for the amendment package or a client-facing summary.

**From:** [Associate]

**Privileged & Confidential: Attorney Work Product**

---

## I. Summary

We act for Stipuv Vertical Holdings, LLC ("**Stipuv**" or "**Buyer**"). Stipuv is the buyer under the Stock Purchase Agreement dated June 30, 2026 (the "**SPA**") with Braveirt Elevator Group, Inc. ("**Braveirt**" or "**Seller**"). It is also the maker of the $7,500,000 Subordinated Promissory Note (the "**Seller Note**"). The deal closed on June 30, 2026 (SPA §3.1). The Purchase Price was $48,500,000 (SPA §2.1), paid as $41,000,000 in cash plus the Seller Note (SPA §2.2).

I reviewed five documents:

- the SPA;
- the Seller Note;
- the Buyer Board of Managers' written consent dated September 14, 2026 (the "**Consent**");
- the Key Employee Agreement with Darnell Okafor-Wyse (the "**KEA**"); and
- the Pellucid Risk Partners certificate cover letter dated July 10, 2026.

The issues are ranked below, most significant first. Three need the client's attention now:

1. **Uncapped Buyer indemnity for Seller Guarantees, including pre-closing defaults** (SPA §§9.3(b), 9.5(c)). Stipuv is the unlimited backstop for Lockwen's pre-closing performance failures under Braveirt's parent guarantees and bonds. There is no cap and no time limit.
2. **The Notice of Disagreement window has already expired** (SPA §2.4(b); Consent Recitals B–C and Resolution 2). The 30-day window closed on **September 3, 2026**, eleven days before the Board authorized the objection. The $1,240,000 working capital surplus claimed by Seller is at risk of being final and binding. **Immediate action is needed.**
3. **The six-month survival period expires long before any set-off is available** (SPA §9.1). The operational representations expire on **December 30, 2026**, which is 55 days from today. The first Seller Note installment, Stipuv's practical source of recovery, is not until **December 31, 2027**. **Protective Claim Notices must go out before December 30.**

Lower-priority items are in Part III. Information we still need is in Part IV.

---

## II. Ranked Issues

### Issue 1: Uncapped indemnity by Buyer for Seller Guarantees, reaching pre-closing defaults

**Where:** SPA §9.3(b), §9.5(a), §9.5(c), §6.8; definition of "Seller Guarantees" in §1.1.

**What the documents say**

- Under §9.3(b), Buyer indemnifies the Seller Indemnitees for all Losses arising from "any Seller Guarantee, including any demand, draw or claim made by any beneficiary … and any payment or performance by Seller … thereunder, *whether arising before, on or after the Closing Date*."
- "Seller Guarantees" is defined broadly. It covers Braveirt's parent performance and payment guarantees, surety and performance bonds and other credit support given to building owners, managing agents and general contractors under Lockwen's maintenance, repair and modernization contracts (Schedule 6.8).
- §9.5(a) caps each side's indemnity at **10% of the Purchase Price ($4,850,000)**. However, §9.5(c) provides that "the limitations in this Section 9.5 *shall not apply to Losses under Section 9.3(b)*." That removes both the cap and every other §9.5 limitation, including the insurance offset in §9.5(d) and the no-double-recovery rule in §9.5(e).
- §6.8 requires Buyer only to use "reasonable efforts" to obtain releases. There is no outside date. Seller must keep each guarantee in place until it is released.

**Why it matters to Stipuv**

- **Risk allocation is inverted.** Suppose a building owner calls a Braveirt guarantee or bond because of a *pre-closing* Lockwen default, such as a missed Category 1 test, defective modernization work or a contract breach before June 30, 2026. Braveirt pays and then recovers the full amount from Stipuv under §9.3(b), with no limit.
- **Stipuv's counter-claim is weak.** Stipuv's claim for the same default would be a representation claim under §9.2(a), relying on §4.9 (Material Customer Contracts), §4.11 or §4.12. That claim is subject to:
  - the $485,000 basket (§9.5(b));
  - the $4,850,000 cap (§9.5(a)); and
  - the six-month survival cut-off (§9.1; see Issue 3).

  After December 30, 2026, the claim is time-barred entirely.
- **The exposure is open-ended.** Because §6.8 has no outside date, the exposure lasts as long as the guaranteed contracts run, including multi-year modernization contracts and auto-renewing maintenance contracts.
- **Size of the exposure.** Performance bonds on modernization work are often sized to full contract value. The exposure could therefore exceed the entire Seller-side cap.

**Recommended fixes**

1. **Seek an amendment to §9.3(b)** limiting it to post-closing events:

   > "(b) any Seller Guarantee, solely to the extent the applicable demand, draw or claim arises out of any act, omission, event or circumstance first occurring after the Closing Date; *provided* that Buyer shall have no obligation under this Section 9.3(b) to the extent such Losses arise out of any matter for which Seller is obligated to indemnify the Buyer Indemnitees under Section 9.2 (determined without regard to the limitations in Section 9.5 or the survival periods in Section 9.1)."

2. **Add a reciprocal Seller indemnity** as a new §9.2(e), covering Losses from any Seller Guarantee claim attributable to pre-closing acts or omissions. This indemnity should not be subject to the cap, basket or survival limits.

3. **Restore a cap or a sunset.** Delete the clause "the limitations in this Section 9.5 shall not apply to Losses under Section 9.3(b)" from §9.5(c). If Braveirt resists, propose a separate stand-alone cap for §9.3(b) together with an outside date (for example, 12 months) after which Seller bears the guarantee risk or must accept Buyer replacement credit support.

4. **Tighten §6.8.** Add a schedule of guarantees, specified replacement steps and an outside date. In return, Seller would cooperate in releases and agree that §9.3(b) exposure ends for any guarantee where Buyer has tendered qualifying replacement support.

5. **Negotiating leverage.** Point out that the provision as drafted lets Seller shift its own pre-closing liability onto Buyer. That outcome is inconsistent with §9.2 and with the commercial bargain.

6. **Immediate operational step.** Ask Lockwen management to:
   - compile Schedule 6.8 with current exposure amounts;
   - identify any guarantee where a pre-closing default is known or suspected; and
   - begin approaching beneficiaries for replacement now.

---

### Issue 2: The Notice of Disagreement window expired before the Board acted

**Where:** SPA §2.4(b); Consent, Recitals B and C and Resolution 2; see also SPA §§2.4(c), 2.4(d), 9.6, 11.2, 11.5.

**What the documents say**

- §2.4(b) requires Buyer to deliver a Notice of Disagreement "within 30 days after Buyer's receipt of the Closing Statement." If Buyer does not, "the Closing Statement shall be final and binding on the parties." Any item not specifically disputed in a *timely* notice is also final.
- Consent Recital B records that Stipuv **received the Closing Statement on August 4, 2026**. The 30-day window therefore **closed on September 3, 2026**.
- The Consent is dated **September 14, 2026**. Recital C states that Stipuv "*has not yet delivered*" a Notice of Disagreement. Resolution 2 only authorizes the officers to prepare and deliver one at that point, eleven days after the deadline.
- The Closing Statement shows a **$1,240,000 surplus payable to Seller** under §2.4(d). Management's position is that Seller wrongly excluded unearned deferred revenue on prepaid maintenance contracts from current liabilities. If that position is correct, the surplus is eliminated or substantially reduced.

**Why it matters to Stipuv**

- **Seller's position is strong.** On the face of §2.4(b), Seller can treat the Closing Statement as final and binding and demand $1,240,000 within five Business Days (§2.4(d)). A payment default on a binding SPA obligation would also create litigation exposure in Manhattan courts (§10.2).
- **The Consent works against us.** It is an internal record of the late date, and it would likely be discoverable.
- **"Manifest error" is not available.** That standard in §2.4(c) applies only to an Independent Accountant determination. It does not apply to an unchallenged Closing Statement.

### Issue 3: The six-month survival period expires about a year before any set-off can be used

**Where:** SPA §9.1, §9.4(a), §9.7; Seller Note §§2(a) and 5(a); SPA §4.12 and §4.9; definition of "Fundamental Representations."

**What the documents say**

- §9.1 provides that all non-Fundamental representations survive only "until *six (6) months after the Closing Date*," which is **December 30, 2026**.
- Fundamental Representations are limited to §§4.1, 4.2, 4.3 and 4.20. They do *not* include:
  - §4.12 (Elevator Code Compliance and Permits);
  - §4.9 (Material Customer Contracts);
  - §4.11 (Compliance with Laws);
  - §4.5 (Financial Statements); or
  - §4.6 (Undisclosed Liabilities).
- Under §9.4(a), a Claim Notice on a representation must be delivered before the survival period ends.
- There is no escrow. Stipuv's practical source of recovery is set-off against the Seller Note (§9.7; Note §5).
- The first Note installment is **$2,500,000 on December 31, 2027** (Note §2(a)).
- Note §5(a) permits set-off *only* for claims "timely asserted by a Claim Notice … before the expiration of the applicable survival period."

**Why it matters to Stipuv**

- **Defects will surface after the claim window closes.** Code and permit defects under §4.12 typically emerge through the annual periodic inspection and Category 1 test cycle, through Category 5 five-year tests, and through DOB or DOL violation notices. Most of the first post-closing cycle will fall after December 30, 2026.
- **Customer contract problems emerge late too.** Problems under §4.9, such as non-renewals, undisclosed defaults or misreported prepaid fees, often emerge at renewal dates that run well into 2027.
- **The result is a remedy gap.** The core operational representations, which drove the price for an elevator maintenance business, expire about a year before the first dollar can be set off. Stipuv would be left suing Seller directly with no security.
- **The gap compounds Issue 1.** Seller's exposure for pre-closing defaults disappears on December 30, 2026, while Stipuv's exposure under §9.3(b) continues indefinitely.

**Recommended actions**

1. **Immediate (before December 30, 2026).**
   - Instruct Lockwen management, including Mr. Okafor-Wyse, to run a focused compliance sweep now: permits, licenses, outstanding violations, test and filing records since January 1, 2023, and Material Customer Contract defaults or non-renewal notices.
   - Deliver protective Claim Notices under §9.4(a) for every known or reasonably suspected breach. Describe each in "reasonable detail" with estimated Losses where known.

   A timely notice preserves both the claim (§9.1, last sentence) and the set-off right (Note §5(a)).

2. **Negotiate an amendment to §9.1.** Extend survival for §§4.5, 4.6, 4.9, 4.11 and 4.12 to at least 18 months after Closing (December 30, 2027). The better position is to run survival to no earlier than 30 days after the first Note installment date, for example:

   > "…All other representations and warranties shall survive the Closing until six (6) months after the Closing Date; *provided* that the representations and warranties in Sections 4.5, 4.6, 4.9, 4.11 and 4.12 shall survive until the later of (i) eighteen (18) months after the Closing Date and (ii) January 31, 2028."

   Note §5(a) would need a conforming amendment so that set-off tracks the extended period.

3. **Alternatives if Seller refuses.**
   - Treat §4.12 as a Fundamental Representation.
   - Add a special indemnity for pre-closing code violations and penalties that does not depend on survival.
   - Seek an escrow or holdback.

   Use Issue 1 as leverage, since Seller benefits from an uncapped, unlimited-duration indemnity in its own favor.
